title: How would you add a cache without serving stale data?
description: Cache-aside with explicit invalidation, TTL discipline, and protection against stampedes and thundering herds.

data.text: Caching is easy to add and hard to get right: the failure mode is users seeing yesterday's price or a deleted account still loading. A correct cache design starts by answering three questions per data type: what is the staleness budget (how wrong can we be, for how long), what events invalidate it, and what happens when the cache is cold or the store is down. 'Set a 10-minute TTL and hope' is an answer to none of them.

The interviewer is testing whether you treat invalidation as a first-class design step and whether you know the failure modes: stampedes when keys expire together, hot-key contention, and the cache becoming a single point of failure. Experienced candidates also say when NOT to cache: rarely-read, expensive-to-cache data, or data where correctness beats latency.
Core pattern: cache-aside with event-driven invalidation

items: Read path: check cache → miss → read database → populate cache → return. The application owns both sides.
Write path: update the database FIRST (it is the source of truth), then evict — not update — the cache entry. Evicting avoids the read-repopulate race writing an old value over a new one.
Invalidate by domain event: after committing the order price change, publish 'product-42-changed' → evict product-42 (and any list keys that embed it).
Staleness budget as configuration: short TTL for prices/inventory (seconds), longer for reference data (hours), near-zero tolerance handled with synchronous invalidation instead of TTL.
List keys are the trap: caching '/products?page=1' means one product change invalidates many pages — tag entries by entity so eviction can target every view that contains it.
Negative caching: cache 'not found' briefly (seconds) to stop repeated misses hammering the DB — but never long enough to resurrect deleted entities incorrectly.

data.title: Read-through with stampede protection

items: Stampede: N requests miss the same expired key simultaneously → single-flight/coalescing (one DB query, others wait).
Thundering herd on restart: cache is empty after deploy → warm it proactively, or serve stale-while-revalidate.
Hot key: one popular key concentrates load on one shard → replicate hot keys, add jitter to TTLs, keep per-key payload small.
Cache down: decide the degradation policy — fall through to the database with a circuit breaker and tight DB timeouts, or serve slightly stale data if the staleness budget allows.
Cache up / DB down: an available cache with a cold DB still answers reads — but be explicit about serving stale data rather than doing it accidentally.
Serialization drift: version your DTOs or accept that schema changes flush the cache on deploy.

data.title: TTL is a staleness budget, not a performance knob
data.text: Every TTL states how wrong your answers may be. Write it down per data type: prices 30s + event invalidation, session data 15m, reference data 24h. If nobody can name the acceptable staleness for a field, the field is not ready to be cached.

In-process (IMemoryCache/HybridCache) is fastest but per-instance and dies on deploy; distributed (Redis) shares state across pods and survives restarts but adds a network hop and serialization; CDN/output caching sits closest to the user for public reads; and pre-aggregated query results (materialized summaries) beat caching when every request recomputes the same expensive aggregate. HybridCache in .NET unifies L1 (in-process) + L2 (distributed) with stampede protection built in — for mixed workloads it is the default you should reach for.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Define the staleness budget per data type before choosing a TTL.
Write to the database first, then evict (not update) the cache.
Invalidate by entity tags/events so list caches can be purged precisely.
Protect against stampedes (single-flight), hot keys (jitter/replication), and outages (degradation policy).
data.takeaway: A cache is correct when invalidation is driven by writes and every TTL is a conscious staleness decision — not when the numbers merely look fast.
